# Here’s what AI leaders are saying about Trump’s new safety plan

﻿Who needs legally binding regulations when you can be your own AI safety judge?

After hosting a meal with Big Tech leaders on Tuesday, President Donald Trump responded to journalist questions about his artificial intelligence announcements in typical fashion. He said his previous claims regarding fears around AI safety being a “hoax” cooked up by Democrats no longer apply now that he’s renamed the technology to “ Super Intelligence .” He brushed off concerns that the government wasn’t enforcing enough AI guardrails because US companies are “dominating China.”

And instead of ushering in federal AI regulations, Trump now has “the smartest people in the world watching over each other.”

The people in question here are Google’s Sundar Pichai, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, XAI’s Elon Musk, and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. These tech leaders have signed the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities : a “morally binding” safety pledge that requires their companies to self-regulate their own AI technology with common sense guidelines and, seemingly, no ramifications for violating the agreement.

All six of the signees provided press commentary at Trump’s behest, praising the self-policing plans as a positive step toward advancing AI technology, creating jobs, and dispersing negative public opinion around AI safety. # The AI Tamagotchis are coming

Personal AI hardware has mostly crashed and burned. OpenAI and Meta are counting on two selling points: It’s useful, and it’s cute.

While AI has made plenty of inroads on people’s phones and computers, it’s largely failed in dedicated devices. But over the next year, two major AI companies, Meta and OpenAI, will attempt to change that. And they’re apparently betting on a similar path: testing appetites for physical hardware with their cutesy software agents.

“Hardware is hard” is a tech industry mantra. Dedicated AI devices like the Friend and Humane AI Pin have inspired mainly frustration and backlash, which may only worsen as public anger toward AI grows. Meta and OpenAI, however, are both pushing ahead. OpenAI is working with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive and plans to ship no earlier than February 2027, per a public filing . Meta aims to launch a pendant-like device sooner, before this year’s holiday shopping season.

While OpenAI’s hardware didn’t make an appearance at this year’s DevDay, the company debuted a major new AI agent platform called Dots, complete with personalizable colored blobs with eyes. During a Q&A with reporters after the keynote, when asked whether Dots would make their way into a future physical hardware device, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman replied that that “seems like a very reasonable thing to assume we may do someday,” declining to offer further details.

Meta, meanwhile, is more directly tying its hardware to the recently released Muse agent. Compared by CEO Mark Zuckerberg to a keychain, the device is called the Muse Charm, and it bears a screen featuring its cuddly-looking Muse AI agent, giving it the air of a Tamagotchi. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” Zuckerberg said onstage . “So, if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you.”

Both OpenAI and Meta have likely learned from other companies’ failed hardware rollouts, and their resulting strategy seems to be soft-launching AI agents before hard-launching the hardware. Their solution for hacking the hardware problem is to prime the market by getting people used to AI agents, hoping people will spread the word that “yes, they really work now.” Once people find value in — and even get attached to — the cutesy agents, they might want them in a more physical form. Other companies, like Friend, have taken similar software-first strategies, but Friend was positioned mainly as a companion chatbot, not a productivity tool.

When asked during the DevDay press Q&A whether Dots will likely become the primary interface for interacting with ChatGPT, Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, said the company would be “evolving ChatGPT in place to be this incredible personal assistant very soon” and that he believes that as people are able to reach their AI agents via email, text, or phone call, the point of interaction is “all going to blur at some point.” It’ll be a “natural part of your life,” Sottiaux said.

Altman is banking on the fact that Dots will be more useful for long-term tasks than previous iterations of agents on the market have been. “This feels like an always-on helper, collaborator … that you can give very large pieces of work to and it gets to know you and helps proactively over time,” he said during the Tuesday press Q&A.

Both companies’ main bet is that, after years of less-than-impressive AI agents, they can finally deliver a useful everyday tool that will break through to a broader public market. But after Muse’s concerning exploits in Facebook Marketplace, and a Dots voice demo that went awry at DevDay, there’s apparently still some work to do.

# OpenAI’s new agent is a shot at Meta — but can it compete with free?

OpenAI and Meta’s cutesy AI agents are about to fight to the death.

At OpenAI’s annual DevDay conference, the company pulled out all the stops to compete with its rivals — primarily Meta, whose Muse AI agent platform has seen early runaway success. CEO Sam Altman walked onstage to cheers and announced Dots, a “real-deal AI” agent powered by GPT-6 Astra, “inspired by the cool agents that we all watched in movies growing up.” Similar to Muse, Dots aims for disarming cuteness, taking the form of colorful, personalizable blobs with eyes. OpenAI fired shots at Meta by demonstrating Dots’ ability to not just act as helpful assistants but build metaverse-esque virtual worlds. But in one key area, Dots strikingly fails to compete: price.

Muse’s main selling point is making AI agent access free and frictionless. The company offers a free dedicated virtual machine that houses both the agent and the user’s associated data. OpenAI’s Dots, by contrast, is restricted for now to users on its $20/month Pro plan and up. While anyone with a Meta account can get Muse, most of ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion users won’t be able to use Dots.

There’s an obvious reason for this: OpenAI likely can’t afford it. The AI lab is reportedly currently aiming to raise $30 billion in funding at a $1.4 trillion valuation, per Bloomberg , and it’s experienced 70 percent growth since the beginning of its third quarter — nearing $70 billion in annual recurring revenue, Axios reported. Yet despite its staggering financing, its funds aren’t limitless, particularly compared to a tech giant like Meta. In the past year, some users have accused AI labs of passing costs on to customers amid an AI money squeeze . OpenAI in particular is burning through a lot of cash right now — it expects to spend $280 billion by 2030, per the FT — and compute is expensive, while it’s also facing pressure from investors to button up its bottom line ahead of going public.

“Dots are starting out as a premium product — it uses a lot of compute,” Altman said Tuesday during a private press Q&A after his DevDay keynote, adding, “I think it will help us understand and help people understand how expansive and what AI can do. But you should of course expect us to do a mass-market thing for billions of people someday.”

During DevDay, OpenAI took pains to explain why Dots (with singular agents referred to as a “Dot”) are worth the money, positioning it as not just a capable personal assistant but a “chief of staff” or experienced engineer. OpenAI employee Holly Li told the audience using a Dot was “like talking to a second brain.” Altman said that Dots were built for delegating “ambitious pieces of work,” like QA for an unreleased product, website design, team offsite trip planning, portfolio rebalancing, and email campaign creation. “Specialist” Dots, trained for areas like accounting and legal analysis, are supposed to launch soon, and the company is working with Microsoft to integrate them into its Agent 365 platform.

The goal, Altman said, is to go beyond agents that simply book reservations, purchase meals, search calendars, and schedule appointments — classic use cases for consumer-facing tools like Muse.

When asked during the press Q&A how Dots is different from Muse and Instinct, another popular new AI agent , Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, said it’s “capable of actually staying on track in very long periods of time.” He added that the multimodality of Dots, which will allow chatting with an agent via text or voice mode and phone call, will feel like “an incredible extension of you.” (The voice demos of Dots didn’t work at DevDay, though, and though OpenAI leaders highlighted the texting-your-agent feature multiple times at the conference, that feature — already supported by Muse and Instinct — is still slated as coming soon.)

Altman said during the Q&A that the long-horizon and knowledge-work tasks were what set Dots apart, adding, “I think this is far beyond anything else available on the market today.” He said that the agents’ help with triaging to-do lists and supporting employees at work would be “difficult for economists to measure right away” but would hopefully make a “huge difference” in how people feel about their jobs.

Framing Dots as a professional tool not only differentiates Dots from Muse, but could help OpenAI gain ground against Anthropic in the enterprise market. Anthropic has focused on — and dominated in — enterprise AI for years, but OpenAI has devoted more resources to the area over the past year. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC that the company’s enterprise business had doubled since July.

OpenAI leads also tried to promote Dots as safer and more secure, particularly compared to Muse. Alexander Embiricos, the company’s Codex product lead, said OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” highlighting that it’s powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s “most aligned model.” During the DevDay keynote, executives also presented “OpenAI Private Intelligence,” a data privacy framework that allows businesses to have “stronger controls” over their data, as well as zero data retention policy options, with no data stored on OpenAI servers.

Altman said onstage that OpenAI hopes to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” The comments come after Muse was recently lambasted for taking over a user’s Facebook Marketplace account and giving out their address to a stranger without the user realizing.

“I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, told The Verge in an interview. “Launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid. I think we’re trying to be really deliberate with how we let our agents use plug-ins, how we let agents use your identity and sign-in/sign up for things, how we let your agents pay for things.”

The question is whether all that is enough to beat free . ChatGPT rose to prominence not only by being first but also by being free — and easy to use even without signing in. Muse may be able to dominate in the AI agent space for the same reason. The other hurdle for making these AI agents as frictionless as possible is that Meta offers easy integration with the other platforms it owns, such as Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. (Google’s Gemini Spark agent platform has an advantage for the same reason.) Though OpenAI said users would be able to connect Dots to a wide range of external tools, they may not be as seamless as an in-house integration.

For now, OpenAI is hoping that a better product will trump a cheaper one. “We might move a tiny bit slower, but we also know that if people have Dots that go out there and YOLO-buy stuff on Facebook Marketplace, that’s just not something we want to put 1.2 billion users through,” Coates said. “We’re trying to do it right, basically.”

# Google’s new Guided Vision feature can help you read the fine print

People with low vision can use Guided Vision to have Gemini describe what’s nearby and ask follow-up questions.

Guided Vision is launching in Gemini Live on compatible Android devices today to use AI to give real-time audio descriptions of anything you point your phone’s camera at. By sharing your camera in Gemini Live, you can have Google’s AI help with things like reading small text, describing your surroundings, finding or identifying objects around you, and describing details on specific objects.

Like the VoiceOver Live Recognition feature Apple has added to the iPhone and Vision Pro , it’s designed for people who are blind, have low vision, or want assistance in specific situations. In addition to the Gemini app, Guided Vision is also available in Google TalkBack, or users can set up an accessibility shortcut for it in the Settings app on devices running Android 9 and above, after it was announced in a recent set of Pixel updates .

You can also ask follow-up questions about whatever you’re looking at, like asking Gemini to read off the expiration date on an item it helped you find. Google says Gemini will give you audio cues to help line up your camera if you ask about something that’s not in the shot. However, Google cautions users not to rely on Guided Vision for things like “navigation, safe-travel guidance, or obstacle detection,” or as a replacement for a cane or mobility aid.

# AI music maker Suno now generates spoken words

﻿The new Speech feature provides synthetic voiceovers embellished with AI background music.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Suno is branching out from the world of AI music, launching a new feature that generates spoken voices based on scripts or prompted descriptions. Speech is now available in public beta across Suno’s web and mobile platforms, and allows you to simultaneously generate voiceovers and background music to accompany them.

“Music will always be at the heart of Suno and what we build. At the same time, our vision has always extended to other forms of human expression,” Suno chief product officer, Jack Brody, said in the announcement. “Today, we’re expanding what’s possible in Suno with Speech: the first audio model that generates voice and music together as one cohesive track.”

AI-generated speech is hardly new — DeepMind has been experimenting with deep learning speech synthesis for a decade, Adobe has a text-to-speech tool, and ElevenLabs has become one of the most recognizable platforms for it since launching in 2023. Suno is just throwing its hat into the ring — likely in an attempt to diversify the platform, given its music generator has attracted so many lawsuits .

Pairing AI music with generated voices is Suno’s spin on text-to-speech tools. It’s optional, meaning you can easily turn off the background music with a toggle if you just want clean speech, but the idea is that it’ll compliment certain use cases for generative spoken word — such as having a calming soundtrack for poems, or something more energetic for dramatic voiceovers and encouraging speeches.

To use the feature, select the “Create” tab, and navigate to the Speech option. There are two modes: Simple, which allows you to describe what you want to create via the provided prompt box (such as “a pirate captain rallying his crew”), or the Advanced mode that lets you add a custom script if you already know exactly what you want it to say. Advanced settings also let you adjust the gender of the AI voice, speech style, and how much variety each voice generation will have. Speech has a maximum duration of around eight minutes.

Suno admits that the feature is far from perfect, but says it’ll keep improving Speech around user feedback. “Beta really does mean beta,” said Brody. “Occasionally, British accents can wander off to Australia and back. Dramatic pauses may be very dramatic. You will almost certainly discover uses for this that never occurred to us.”

# Inside our months-long investigation into Kevin O’Leary’s Utah data center debacle

Verge features writer Josh Dzieza discusses his investigation into the Stratos data center, and how Utah residents fought back against it.

Today I’m talking with Josh Dzieza, a longtime features writer here at The Verge , about Kevin O’Leary’s plans to build a massive data center in Utah .

The idea was to build the world’s biggest data center — a 40,000-acre AI campus with nine gigawatts of power, or more than double the average power usage of the entire state of Utah. The project is technically called Stratos, but it’s more prominently known as Wonder Valley, a reference to O’Leary’s nickname on Shark Tank .

Josh has spent months reporting on this project, and it’s fair to say Wonder Valley has completely upended Utah politics. What Josh found throughout the course of his reporting was that the way this data center came together — how it was planned, how it was announced and approved, and how local residents were kept in the dark — ultimately created a political firestorm so severe it stopped Stratos in its tracks.

Now, the details of what happened with Wonder Valley are obviously fascinating. But the story is also a larger look at the AI industry’s infrastructure boom, the bipartisan backlash to that buildout, and how the tech industry is running into the one obstacle it can’t seem to spend its way out of: local democracy.

Okay: The Verge ’s Josh Dzieza on the Utah data center disaster. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Josh Dzieza, you are a features writer here at The Verge . Welcome to Decoder .

Thanks for having me.

I’m very excited to talk to you. For people who don’t know, Josh has one of the hardest jobs at The Verge . You just disappear for long periods of time, and then you come back with 15,000-word home runs, which is an enormous amount of pressure, but you keep hitting them.

It’s a great job. [ Verge features editor] Kevin Nguyen might say that editing those 15,000 words down to something manageable is the hardest job, but it’s all fun.

The home run we sent you out to get this time was the story of what happened with Kevin O’Leary in Utah, where he promised to build what was going to be the biggest data center in the world.

He was all over the news talking about building the biggest data center in the world, it was called Stratos. He was calling the entire development Wonder Valley. This thing fell apart in a bunch of anger from the local community. There’s a defamation lawsuit because O’Leary referred to all of his critics as Chinese spies on Fox News. Fox News had to apologize on the air .

Josh, when you started reporting on this story, it struck me that there would be some similarities to the huge feature you wrote about the Foxconn project in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, my hometown, where President Trump announced that Foxconn was going to build a massive LCD factory in the middle of Wisconsin. There were supposed to be 13,000 jobs, and none of that happened.

Actually, what’s funny about that is now that land is being used for a Microsoft data center , which is just maybe the natural end state of all things. Walk me through the parallels and differences at a high level. What did this feel like to report?

I did not expect this to feel so similar to Foxconn initially, because unlike the Foxconn project, the data center buildout is real and at least theoretically can make sense in many cases. These things are actually getting built — unlike an LCD fab in the middle of Wisconsin. It turned out that there are more parallels than I thought.

I mean, one, just the actors that you have that takes place mostly with local officials and planning meetings and angry residents and things like that. But also there’s a lot more data centers on paper and speculation, things that are maybe real and maybe not that are more difficult to suss out than I was fully aware of going into data center reporting.

Let’s start at the very start of this project. There’s an enormous cast of characters involved. There’s a whole bunch of government agencies, but this starts with people in Utah looking at 40,000 acres of empty space and realizing that something is about to happen.

We can start with the beginning of the project, which is several months before anyone had any idea anything was happening, including most people in Utah — except for a handful of people who own property in this remote valley, some people in the state government at this one agency that became involved and a few real estate developers.

So everyone except maybe a dozen or so people found out about this project when Kevin O’Leary starts talking about it as an enormous data center that he’s building in Utah called Wonder Valley, or sometimes Stratos, depending on what program word they’re using at the moment.

O’Leary comes out in late April and says, “We’re building this giant thing,” and that’s the first time most people in the county, and in the state, had heard about it.

How did Kevin O’Leary get the approvals to even begin saying he was going to start building this data center so publicly if no one knew about it?

It is partly because it ran through an agency called MIDA (Military Installation Development Authority), which is like a state development agency that deals with projects that have some military purpose.

I think the military purpose can be fairly tangential. MIDA has a luxury ski resort that gives veterans discounts, but it began as a way to create projects on military property that was unused or could be put to more economic use. And then the taxes go back to the state, some of which can fund military developments. It also has a lot of power to override local land use. It basically becomes the municipal government in whatever project area it establishes.

So if it establishes a project area, in theory, it would really speed up all the permitting and zoning and other regulations that can be a huge problem for data center projects. In order to establish a project area, the board has to ratify it and all the landowners in the area have to give their consent and then the local government — in this case, the county — has to give its consent.

The issue with this is by the time Kevin O’Leary is talking about it on Fox in late April, MIDA has approved it. The county has not. The county didn’t even know about it until about a month before this happened.

So did Kevin O’Leary just go to this obscure military agency and say, “I need a bunch of land in Utah,” and get it?

According to the documents we have, he starts asking around at the state level with the governor in early January. Then, the project gets passed from the governor’s office to MIDA. So in January to February, he’s basically going around, which is not uncommon with these developers, state to state saying, “I want to build a data center, what have you got?” Whoever gives the best pitch, the best, “You can have this property, we’re going to make permitting easy. We have these tax breaks,” wins.

This is also quite similar to what we saw with Foxconn, and a lot of big development projects. People do this sort of beauty pageant thing: “We’re auditioning this state, we’re auditioning this state. It’s a race, it’s a competition. Who’s going to win?” So there’s some of that going on there.

O’Leary has been very publicly out in front. His big defense of the project is, “Well, states compete with these tax breaks, and Utah gave me these tax breaks.” Somewhere in there is a big disconnect from the actual people living in the area and the process.

I mean, that’s the conflict here, that’s the real heart of the story is eventually the people in the area find out this is happening, and they don’t want it to happen and they mount furious pushback. What happened there?

It’s a really interesting case with Stratos, where all of the conversations until very late are happening at the developer and state level. In this case, they literally forgot or failed or for some reason did not tell the county government, whose consent they needed, that this was happening until very late. So that happens in late March, and the county commissioners start hearing rumors that apparently there’s a data center coming. They have no idea. They ask around and the state says, “We’re sorry, we forgot to tell you essentially, but we really need your approval fast.”

The county commissioners then have a meeting in late April, and that’s when word starts to trickle out, and then MIDA votes to approve it two days later. Over that weekend in late April, you’ve now had two public meetings, there’s local coverage, people start talking about it saying, “Oh, did you hear about the data center?” Several people found out about it at the coffee shop, at the grocery store. They just hear about it on Facebook. They’re like, “Oh, there’s a big data center coming. For some reason, the Shark Tank guy is involved.” That starts to trickle out in late April, when you start to see that conversation happen.

No one was happy about it. One of the interesting things about data centers right now is social media is so full of data center backlash stories. # AI hallucinations are making entitled customers even worse

Thanks to AI, the customer really isn’t always right.

Madison, a server in New York City, greets every table by asking about each diner’s allergies. Lately, there have been some close calls. “Sometimes people will tell me they have a shellfish allergy, and I’ll come back, and they won’t ask me any questions,” says Madison, who asked that her last name be withheld to protect her identity. “And they’ll order a fish dish that comes with a broth that is made of shellfish.”

When she tells them a dish contains an allergen, she’s had guests push back, saying ChatGPT disagrees. “They just want to talk to ChatGPT,” Madison explains. “You’re allergic to shellfish, and ChatGPT says there’s no shellfish in this, and we are telling you, yes there is!”

Mass adoption of generative AI tools is rewriting the old adage that has long been a thorn in the side of restaurant and retail workers: “The customer is always right.” But what happens when the customer expects you to play along with something AI made up?

Beyond ignoring her warnings about allergens, Madison has noticed an increased reliance on generative AI among patrons at the Michelin-recommended Italian restaurant where she worked until recently. “The amount of times I’ve suggested, ‘Let me grab the sommelier for you,’ and they say, ‘No, I’ll just ask ChatGPT,’ or somms have been dismissed from the table because the guest has a preference for ChatGPT, that has been increasing quite a bit,” she says. She’s had customers request bottles that the restaurant doesn’t carry — or, in some cases, that don’t exist at all.

For Madison, these AI hallucinations exacerbate some people’s preexisting anxieties about wine. “Some people have always had an issue with sommeliers, thinking ‘These people are like used car salesmen trying to get us to spend way more than we want to on a bottle of wine,’” she says, “or there are people who get in their heads and think, ‘The sommelier is going to think I’m stupid.’” To “soften the blow” of AI hallucinations, Madison and her colleagues will say things like, “We have this really hyper-specific wine list, maybe it’s showing you a French wine, and we don’t carry French wine,” instead of telling the customer their AI chatbot completely made up a wine brand.

You’re allergic to shellfish, and ChatGPT says there’s no shellfish in this, and we are telling you, yes there is!

The AI creep is seemingly ubiquitous in customer service jobs now. The launch of Muse, Meta’s new AI agent, will likely exacerbate the issue — and the headaches for workers who have to field customers’ occasionally nonsensical requests. In reporting this story, I heard from movie theater workers, baristas, and Apple Store employees, all of whom have had customers ask for products or features that don’t exist. On Reddit and X, customer service workers are complaining about customers who take ChatGPT’s word as gospel.

Jason, a river ranger who works on federal lands in the Mountain West, says he’s noticed an increase in visitors arriving to the park with nonsensical AI-generated itineraries.

“My colleagues and I have explained that the AI hallucinated campsites or scheduled things out of geographical order, so the group would have to row their boats upstream some days (not possible) and float with the river current other days,” says Jason, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym because he’s a federal employee. “The craziest part is that even with a ranger explaining this while pointing at a map, we’ve had multiple groups remain skeptical. A certain type of AI user is inclined to trust ChatGPT over rangers, maps, and printed guidebooks.”

Casey, an after-school program teacher in New York who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym, says she’s noticed many students’ parents, nannies, and other caretakers are now turning to ChatGPT or Claude for their questions on childhood development.

“We had one family that consulted ChatGPT to come up with a bedtime routine and sleep schedule for their kid, but their kid wasn’t getting quite enough sleep,” Casey says. Based on his behavior in the program, Casey estimated that the child needed two to three more hours of sleep a night, and told his parents this. “The parents just insisted that their ChatGPT was telling them that their schedule was fine.”

Some parents, she says, now see generative AI tools as experts whose knowledge surpasses that of childcare professionals. “It can be really hard to talk with somebody who has made their mind up,” Casey says, “because they trust this outside entity as being invaluable.” She’s also noticed more anodyne uses of the technology, like kids coming in with AI-generated coloring sheets.

Lauren Wilford, who has worked in food service for 15 years, has noticed AI creeping into her recent interactions with guests as well. It started with the menu: Someone would upload a photo of it to ChatGPT or Claude and ask it what to order, or for guidance on a wine pairing, instead of asking the server.

But now, it appears, some customers have dropped the intermediary altogether. Over the past year, Wilford’s restaurant has been getting calls and emails from agents trying to make reservations on users’ behalf. The rise of agentic AI makes these interactions that much more confusing.

Wilford was surprised when a hands-off client suddenly became demanding on the eve of a big event, making last-minute requests for podiums and AV equipment — neither of which were readily available at the Providence, Rhode Island, restaurant she manages — and eleventh-hour changes to the catering menu. But Wilford was even more taken aback when the clients arrived the next day and didn’t mention any of it. Though she can’t prove it, Wilford believes the requests may not have come from anyone at the company at all; she suspects they were the work of an AI agent.

“I’m sympathetic to the reasons people use AI agents,” Wilford says, especially for bureaucratic and administrative tasks. “But anything where there’s value to two humans seeing each other and working something out together, I think we’re not sensitive to what might be lost if we try to skip all of that stuff.”

# If a data center is camouflaged in the woods, will anyone hate it?

Microsoft is expanding ‘biomimicry’ at its data centers as it faces more pushback from locals over construction, pollution, and noise.

San Antonio City Councilmember Ric Galvan remembers when data centers first arrived in his city in the 2000s, looking like relatively unassuming office buildings. But that’s changed in recent years, as data centers have grown into massive “hyperscale” facilities spanning millions of square feet and housing the physical infrastructure for AI.

There are now more than a dozen data centers in Galvan’s roughly 55-square-mile district, and he expects that number to grow to around 20 over the next few years if proposed projects are completed. They’re clustered along two main roads, concentrating nuisances in the same neighborhoods: traffic and trees cut down during construction, followed by constant bright lights and noise when the data center is operating.

A lot of the area used to be green fields, he explains, allowing many residents to feel close to nature. Now, he says, “that [feeling] gets taken away pretty quickly when you make a gigantic data center.”

“That [feeling] gets taken away pretty quickly when you make a gigantic data center.”

Across the US, more and more communities are rising up against these hulking data warehouses — protesting the effects they could have on quality of life, pollution, water, and electricity bills. Tech companies have responded with promises to mitigate any potential harm by paying for infrastructure upgrades needed in local water and power systems.

Microsoft is also taking a different approach to soften the impact its data centers have. It announced plans to make its data centers less jarring to local communities and the environment through what it describes as “ biomimicry .”

Biomimicry is sort of a catch-all term for many of the ways technologies take inspiration from nature, from “painless” needles that imitate a mosquito’s proboscis to naturally ventilated buildings modeled after termite mounds . In Microsoft’s case, biomimicry involves “blending our datacenters into the natural landscape” to “create resilient ecosystems that support biodiversity, strengthen community ties, and help our datacenters become better neighbors.”

Essentially, Microsoft wants to make its data centers greener, literally, with more gardens and native trees on-site. It’s also promising to invest in projects that repair damaged ecosystems where it has data centers. The company thinks these efforts will limit problems its facilities have caused for neighbors, like noise pollution and the loss of green space.

It’s a nice gesture, advocates and sustainability experts tell me. Microsoft has tried to set itself apart from its rivals by engaging more with communities where it builds data centers. The strategy has appeased some local concerns — depending on whom you ask.

But these data centers are expanding so fast that they’ve simultaneously razed thousands of trees, and Microsoft’s greenhouse gas emissions are growing with the energy demands of AI. Advocates and residents near these data centers want to see more from the company to limit its larger impact on communities and the environment.

## Zooming in

“Maybe … they’re trying to just make sure that they’re covering their bases,” Galvan says. “But also, I think if that’s the case, that’s fine,” he adds — as long as Microsoft and other data center operators are actually addressing concerns residents have brought up for years around pollution, water use, and the destruction of natural green spaces.

Microsoft has operated data centers in the Greater San Antonio area for almost a decade, and is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to build several more . In 2022, the company upset residents in San Antonio when it cut down more than 2,600 trees across a 33-acre expanse to build a data center. That — along with Microsoft’s requests for a zoning change and tax incentive — was a big controversy, Galvan says.

“We’re very proud of our trees here,” Galvan says, pointing out that the tree canopy also helps to mitigate heat, which in Texas is a growing problem. “So it was very frustrating to see that completely decimated.” (In an email, Microsoft spokesperson Jennifer Lyons that the company is “investing in enhancement projects that includes 400+ acres of woodland and pollinator prairie restoration” in San Antonio with a goal of leaving “land more productive than we received it.”)

“We’re actually customizing the solutions to fit in with the local habitat and enhance what’s already there and restore what might have been lost in the past,” Kaitlin Chuzi, director of global land strategy at Microsoft, says.

In its September announcement, Microsoft references successes it has had in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin , where the company is repurposing the shuttered Foxconn LCD factory property for its own data centers. In 2023, Microsoft funded a $4.2 million project to restore the flow of a creek that runs through its property, working with the Root-Pike Watershed Initiative Network (Root-Pike WIN) to do so — an example of the company working with locals to restore ecosystems.

Root-Pike WIN executive director Dave Giordano was also pleasantly surprised to see Microsoft outfit stormwater ponds on its property with forebays to prevent sediment from escaping. “That’s rare around here,” he says. “Not all data center companies are the same. Councilmember Galvan also acknowledges that Microsoft has made itself more approachable by employing a local representative for the company who responds to community concerns. “That’s very different than other data centers in our city,” he says. “I have nothing bad to say about nature-based solutions that are sensitive to the native ecosystem,” says Adrian Shelley, Texas director at consumer advocacy group Public Citizen. “All of that is good and is positive. However, I think that it’s, you know, basically lipstick on a pig.”

Greg Abbott has also imposed statewide moratoriums on data center projects seeking to connect to the power grid pending audits on their electricity and water use.

Data centers often use water in cooling systems needed to keep servers from overheating.
